```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

Age groups are analytical choices. Their boundaries determine which differences
remain visible and which are combined into a single summary. Choose boundaries
that preserve distinctions relevant to your question, support reliable estimates,
and permit the intended comparisons.

This vignette follows one decision: how much childhood detail to retain when
reporting pertussis incidence. You will compare three schemes, examine what
pooling conceals, and document a choice. It assumes familiarity with R data
frames and with age values and intervals; see [Understanding agecraft
classes](classes.html) for those concepts.

## Start with the question

A scheme suitable for describing a population may be unsuitable for measuring
vaccination timeliness. Establish the measure and comparison before choosing
boundaries.

| Task | What should determine the boundaries? |
| --- | --- |
| Disease surveillance | Age-related occurrence, exposure, and the reporting question |
| Vaccination coverage | The age by which receipt is assessed and the eligible cohort |
| Population description | The demographic structure and detail needed for comparison |
| Age adjustment | Compatible age-specific rates and standard-population weights |

CDC's archived [surveillance guidance][cdc-surveillance] gives a childhood
pattern of under 1, 1–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, and 20+. This is historical teaching
guidance, not a universal current reporting requirement or a vaccination
schedule. The [CDC pertussis teaching example][cdc-pertussis] illustrates why
separating infants from ages 1–4 can matter.

## Preserve differences that matter

To examine that consequence, use the following **synthetic data**. Each row is
one completed year of age in a fictional population during the same one-year
period. The counts deliberately illustrate higher infant incidence; they are
not CDC observations or estimates of present-day pertussis risk. Population
values represent compatible annual population denominators for this example.

```{r teaching-data}
pertussis <- data.frame(
  age_year = 0:19,
  cases = c(40, rep(5, 4), rep(3, 5), rep(4, 5), rep(2, 5)),
  population = rep(10000, 20)
)
pertussis$age <- age(pertussis$age_year, unit = "year")
```

Here a completed age of zero identifies the under-one interval. The integer
coordinates are sufficient because all the proposed cutpoints are whole years.
They would not support splitting infants into month-based groups.

Construct the complete schemes, including their adult and terminal intervals,
then display only childhood rates. The first follows CDC's childhood pattern;
the other two use uniform bands ending at 85+ and 90+, respectively. Those
terminal groups are explicit teaching choices.

```{r define-schemes}
make_bands <- function(breaks, labels = NULL) {
  intervals <- age_interval(head(breaks, -1), tail(breaks, -1), unit = "year")
  if (is.null(labels)) {
    starts <- head(breaks, -1)
    ends <- tail(breaks, -1)
    labels <- ifelse(is.infinite(ends), paste0(starts, "+"),
                     paste0(starts, "-", ends - 1))
  }
  names(intervals) <- labels
  intervals
}

childhood <- age_scheme(
  make_bands(c(0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, Inf),
             c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20+")),
  id = "cdc_childhood_teaching", name = "CDC childhood teaching pattern",
  domain = c(0, Inf), complete = TRUE,
  purpose = "Preserve infant and childhood distinctions in a teaching analysis",
  organization = "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention",
  source = "Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 5, Section 5 (archived)",
  reference = paste0("https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/",
                     "ss1978/lesson5/section5.html"),
  verified = FALSE,
  notes = "Historical teaching pattern; source edition not recorded. Not a vaccine schedule."
)
five_year <- age_scheme(
  make_bands(c(seq(0, 85, 5), Inf)),
  id = "five_year_teaching", name = "Five-year teaching bands",
  domain = c(0, Inf), complete = TRUE,
  purpose = "Compare pooling infants with ages 1-4"
)
ten_year <- age_scheme(
  make_bands(c(seq(0, 90, 10), Inf)),
  id = "ten_year_teaching", name = "Ten-year teaching bands",
  domain = c(0, Inf), complete = TRUE,
  purpose = "Compare further pooling of childhood ages"
)
schemes <- list("Childhood pattern" = childhood,
                "Five-year bands" = five_year, "Ten-year bands" = ten_year)
```

The published pattern is attributed, while `verified = FALSE` avoids claiming
a verified source edition that has not been recorded. Neither uniform scheme
is presented as an institutional standard.

For each scheme, assign the same age rows and add their counts and populations.
This is exact aggregation: every source row falls wholly within one destination
interval. No population is divided across a boundary.

```{r calculate-rates}
summarize_rates <- function(scheme) {
  group <- categorize_age(pertussis$age, by = scheme)
  totals <- aggregate(pertussis[c("cases", "population")],
                      by = list(group = group), FUN = sum)
  totals$rate <- 100000 * totals$cases / totals$population
  totals
}
rates <- lapply(schemes, summarize_rates)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rates), function(view) {
  data.frame(view = view, rates[[view]], row.names = NULL)
})), digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
caption = "Synthetic childhood incidence per 100,000 population")
```

Infant incidence is 400 per 100,000 in these data. Pooling ages 0–4 produces
120 per 100,000; pooling ages 0–9 produces 75 per 100,000. The observations
have not changed. The summaries answer progressively broader questions and
conceal the infant contrast. Actual data need not show this same pattern.

```{r compare-rates, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, fig.alt="Three point plots on a common rate scale show the synthetic infant rate of 400 falling to 120 in ages 0-4 and 75 in ages 0-9."}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
for (view in names(rates)) {
  result <- rates[[view]]
  plot(seq_len(nrow(result)), result$rate, xaxt = "n", pch = 19,
       ylim = c(0, 420), xlab = "Age group (years)",
       ylab = "Cases per 100,000", main = view)
  axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(result)), labels = result$group, las = 2)
}
par(old_par)
```

These points represent interval-specific rates, not a continuous age curve.
Equally spaced labels do not imply equal interval widths. A common vertical
scale keeps the comparison visible without using bar areas to represent rates.

The pooled rate is a population-weighted combination of component rates:

\[
R = 100{,}000\frac{\sum_i C_i}{\sum_i N_i}.
\]

Do not average rates without their populations. For under 1 and ages 1–4 here,
the simple mean of 400 and 50 would be 225, whereas their pooled rate is 120.

## Check whether the denominators support the choice

Preserving infant detail requires both infant cases and an infant denominator.
A population total for ages 0–4 cannot supply separate under-one and 1–4
populations without further information or an estimation assumption. Match age
bounds, geography, period, and relevant population characteristics before
calculating rates. CDC's [surveillance guidance][cdc-surveillance] specifically
warns against mismatched case and population age categories.

Keep the finest suitable source ages when permitted. Aggregating compatible
single-year populations to broader groups is possible; recovering single-year
populations from ten-year totals is not an exact operation. Interval crosswalks
can identify overlap but do not justify allocating aggregate counts.

## Balance detail against precision

Narrow groups can expose a useful difference while producing uncertain estimates.
Review counts alongside rates and use confidence intervals appropriate to the
measure and study design. There is no universal minimum count that makes every
rate reliable. Zero observed cases also do not establish absence of risk.

This teaching display omits uncertainty to isolate the effect of pooling. In an
actual report, assess uncertainty before choosing a reporting resolution. You
might combine periods, retain detail with uncertainty intervals, or combine
adjacent groups and state the detail lost. Avoid selecting boundaries solely to
produce a striking contrast.

An infant analysis in months could address vaccination opportunities, but needs
suitable age precision, denominators, and a separately cited schedule version.
Coverage achieved by a milestone is a different measure from incidence within
an age interval. Calculate age in the target calendar unit from the original
dates where needed; do not assume a fixed number of days per month.

## Preserve the comparisons you need

When comparing reports, check definitions and editions as well as labels.
[NCI SEER's age-adjustment tutorial][seer] illustrates why: it describes a
20-group standard ending in 85–89 and 90+, alongside an earlier 19-group
arrangement ending at 85+. An age-adjusted comparison requires compatible
age groups, standard-population weights, and methods. A scheme object supplies
definitions; it does not calculate an age-adjusted rate or establish that its
weights and denominators are appropriate.

If mandatory reporting bands hide a relevant distinction, consider retaining
the required summary and providing a supplementary detailed view with its
limitations stated.

## Make boundaries and rationale explicit

In agecraft, intervals include their lower endpoint and exclude their upper
endpoint. Ages 1–4 mean `[1, 5)` years, including 4.9; a value exactly 5 belongs
to the next interval. An open-ended group uses `Inf` as its upper bound.

```{r boundary-example}
categorize_age(age(c(0.9, 1, 4.9, 5, NA), unit = "year"), by = childhood)
```

The missing age remains unassigned. All three schemes cover nonnegative finite
ages, so valid age values have a match. With partial coverage, an unmatched age
also gives a missing assignment; `classify_age_scheme()` can distinguish missing
input from unmatched input in its status column.

For this teaching question, retain the childhood pattern because it exposes the
infant distinction and the synthetic denominators support it. Document that
rationale alongside the source and any adaptations. Purpose explains why a
scheme was selected; provenance records where it came from and its history.
Use `purpose` for the intended analysis and `notes` for rationale, caveats, or
adaptations that lack a dedicated field.

Before adopting a scheme, record the question, the risk distinctions retained,
denominator compatibility, uncertainty, intended comparisons, and boundary
rules. These are analytical decisions; they need not all become class fields.
Save the scheme with the analysis because classified `age_group` results retain
interval definitions but do not retain scheme provenance. See the
[classes vignette](classes.html#the-age_scheme-class-a-reusable-definition-with-context)
for the storage model and [Reusable age schemes](age-schemes.html) for validation
and derivative tracking.

[cdc-surveillance]: https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson5/section5.html
[cdc-pertussis]: https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson1/section6.html
[seer]: https://seer.cancer.gov/seerstat/tutorials/aarates/definition.html
